concept.body: Choosing a similarity criterion: know two ANGLES → AA; know two proportional SIDES and the angle BETWEEN them → SAS~; know all THREE proportional sides → SSS~. Look for free parts first: a shared angle is equal to itself, and parallel lines create equal corresponding angles (often enabling AA).

explanationVariants: With only angle information, AA is the criterion — two equal angles suffice.
No sides given means AA, the angle-only criterion.

widget.prompt: You know two pairs of equal angles and no side lengths. Which criterion proves similarity?

options.label: AA
options.feedback: Two equal angle pairs is exactly AA — no sides needed.

options.label: SAS~
options.feedback: SAS~ needs side lengths for the proportion. With only angles, use AA.

options.label: SSS~
options.feedback: SSS~ needs three side ratios. Only angles are given, so AA.

options.label: SSS congruence
options.feedback: That needs equal sides and gives congruence. Two equal angles → AA similarity.

steps.body: Three similarity criteria, one decision. **AA** when you know two angles. **SAS~** when you know two proportional sides and the angle between them. **SSS~** when you know all three sides. Inventory what's given — and what's free (shared angles are equal, parallel lines make equal angles) — then pick the criterion whose pattern you can complete.

widget.prompt: Sort each situation by the similarity criterion it fits.

items.label: Two pairs of equal angles
items.feedback: Two equal angles is exactly AA — the third follows from the angle sum.

items.label: Two proportional sides and the included angle equal
items.feedback: Proportional sides with the angle between them is SAS~.

items.label: Three pairs of proportional sides
items.feedback: All three sides proportional is SSS~ — no angle needed.

items.label: A shared angle and the two sides around it proportional
items.feedback: The shared (equal) angle is included between the proportional sides — SAS~.

widget.missFeedback: Count what you're given: angles only → AA; two sides + included angle → SAS~; three sides → SSS~.
widget.successFeedback: Match the given parts to the criterion's pattern.

explanationVariants: Parallel lines cut by a transversal make equal corresponding (or alternate) angles — a free angle pair, often setting up AA.
A parallel line inside a triangle creates equal angles with the base, handing you AA.

widget.prompt: A line parallel to one side of a triangle crosses the other two sides. Which criterion does this most naturally set up?

options.label: AA similarity from corresponding angles
options.feedback: Parallel lines make equal corresponding angles, giving two equal angle pairs — AA similarity.

options.label: SSS similarity from proportional sides
options.feedback: You aren't handed three side ratios directly; the parallel line gives equal ANGLES, pointing to AA.

options.label: SAS congruence from two sides and an angle
options.feedback: This is a SIMILARITY setup (the small triangle is a scaled copy), and it comes from equal ANGLES: AA.

options.label: No valid criterion from parallel lines
options.feedback: Parallel lines are very helpful — they create the equal angles that make AA work.

steps.body: Once similar, the payoff is a **proportion**. Write corresponding sides as equal ratios and solve for the unknown — cross-multiply. The hardest part is usually matching corresponding sides correctly; the similarity statement's letter order (or the figure's angle marks) tells you which side pairs with which.

widget.prompt: △ABC ~ △DEF. AB = 8 corresponds to DE = 12, and BC = 10. Find EF.

commonErrors.feedback: 14 = 10 + 4 adds the difference (12 − 8). Use the ratio 12/8 = 1.5: EF = 10 × 1.5 = 15.
6.67 = 10 × 8/12 inverts the ratio. DEF is larger, so EF = 10 × 12/8 = 15.

explanationVariants: When only angle information is available, AA is the quickest — no sides required.
Two equal angles is the lightest route to similarity: AA.

widget.prompt: You can see two pairs of equal angles but have NO side lengths. Which criterion should you use?

options.label: AA
options.feedback: AA needs only two equal angle pairs — perfect when no sides are known.

options.label: SAS~
options.feedback: SAS~ requires side lengths for the proportion — you have none. Use AA.

options.label: SSS~
options.feedback: SSS~ needs all three side ratios — impossible without lengths. AA uses only angles.

options.label: None — you need at least one side
options.feedback: AA needs NO sides at all. Two equal angle pairs is enough.

steps.body: A reliable proof recipe: (1) mark everything given plus the free parts; (2) name the criterion whose pattern is complete; (3) state the similarity; (4) write the proportion for the target; (5) solve. Similarity proofs are shorter than congruence proofs — often just one criterion and one proportion.

widget.prompt: DE ∥ BC in △ABC (D on AB, E on AC). Prove △ADE ~ △ABC. Order the steps.

items.label: Therefore AD/AB = AE/AC (corresponding sides of similar triangles)

misorderFeedback.feedback: The AA conclusion needs both equal angle pairs stated first — the corresponding-angles line comes before it.
The side proportion follows FROM the similarity, so △ADE ~ △ABC must be established first.

widget.missFeedback: Two equal angles (corresponding + shared), conclude AA similarity, then write the side proportion.
widget.successFeedback: Equal angles → AA → similar → proportional sides.

steps.body: See the ratios stay locked before you compute them.

widget.prompt: DE ∥ BC in △ABC (D on AB, E on AC). Slide the cutter to six tenths of the way from A toward B, so AD is 1.5 times DB, then read what AE/EC is forced to do.
widget.successFeedback: Both readouts show 1.50. AD/DB = 0.6/0.4 = 1.5, and AE/EC matches it exactly — the same ratio the challenge below uses to solve for AC.
widget.lowFeedback: Too early — AD/DB is still under 1.5. Keep sliding toward B; watch AE/EC follow AD/DB the whole way, never lagging behind.
widget.highFeedback: Past it — AD/DB has climbed above 1.5. Ease back toward A; notice overshooting moved AE/EC by the same amount, never just one ratio alone.

hints: The parallel line gives you AA similarity between the small and large triangle.
Set up AD/AB = AE/AC with the known lengths.
AD=6, AB=6+4=10, AE=9; solve 6/10 = 9/AC... careful: AE corresponds to full AC.
explanationVariants: By AA (parallel line), △ADE ~ △ABC, so AD/AB = AE/AC: 6/10 = 9/AC gives AC = 9 × 10 ÷ 6 = 15.

widget.prompt: In △ABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC. AD = 6, DB = 4, and AE = 9. Find AC.

commonErrors.feedback: 13 = 9 + 4 adds the wrong pieces. Use AD/AB = AE/AC: 6/10 = 9/AC → AC = 15.
5.4 = 9 × 6 ÷ 10 solves an inverted ratio. Set 6/10 = 9/AC → AC = 9 × 10 ÷ 6 = 15.

takeaways: AA for angles, SAS~ for two sides + included angle, SSS~ for three sides.
Free parts: shared angles (reflexive), parallel-line angles.
Prove similar, then write and solve a proportion for the unknown.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: a parallel line splits two sides proportionally — the side-splitter theorem.
